messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 43
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Vignette:
Clara’s life fractured on a Tuesday in November when her body turned against her in a way no recipe could compensate for. One moment she was plating scallops at the pass, the next she was on a gurney in a crowded emergency department, gasping as a tube was forced down her throat. The months that followed were a blur of fluorescent lights, the rhythmic hiss of a ventilator, and the cold weight of monitoring straps across her ribs. She remembered the sheer helplessness of lying still while strangers adjusted her breathing, the metallic taste of fear in her mouth, and the terrifying realization that she could no longer trust the muscles she had relied on for two decades. The memory was so extreme that she still caught herself wondering if she had imagined it, yet the grief that accompanied the recall was a physical weight in her chest, heavy and suffocating. In the weeks after discharge, Clara’s physiology refused to settle. Before her mind could register that she was home in her own bed, her pulse would spike, her chest would tighten, and her palms would sweat. She stood in her kitchen one morning and suddenly felt the phantom pressure of the endotracheal tube, the sterile smell of antiseptic flooding her nose, the sharp beep of a cardiac monitor echoing in her skull. She would drop her spoon and grip the counter, certain the crisis was happening again. The memory never arrived as a simple thought; it crashed over her all at once, a full sensory reliving that left her shaking. Even when she knew she was in a safe place, her shoulders remained braced, her breath shallow, entirely unable to relax. What frightened her most was the conviction that she had crossed a threshold from which she could not return. She believed her body had been permanently damaged, a traitor that would never stop sounding alarms. She believed she would never feel normal emotions again, that the capacity for quiet joy had been burned out. Over the following months, her days became structured around a series of parallel withdrawals. She stayed awake until three in the morning, scrolling through her phone until her eyes burned, just to outrun the silence where the memories waited. When she felt a wave of relief or the first stirrings of hope, she would deliberately pull back, guarding herself against the vulnerability of anticipation. She stopped looking forward to weekend getaways with her partner, Mark, telling herself she was too tired, though the truth was she could not bear the feeling of opening up to happiness again. In the kitchen, the sensory landscape remained unchanged, yet everything felt dangerous. The sudden clatter of a dropped pan sounded like a crash cart rolling down a hallway. The whistle of a pressure cooker made her shoulders lock. She began taking shorter shifts, then leaving early, missing staff dinners because she could not bear the sight of colleagues celebrating around a cake. Her head chef noticed the distance in her movements, the way she flinched when a nurse in scrubs walked through the back door to drop off supplies. By spring, the weight had become unbearable. She found herself staring at her own hands while chopping vegetables, feeling a profound disconnect from the very organs that once built her career. What finally brought her to the clinic was not a single panic attack, but the quiet realization that she had stopped eating her own food, that she had stopped laughing with Mark, and that the safety of her own apartment no longer felt safe. She did not know if she was hoping to feel the grief lift, or simply to find a way to let her body stop fighting her. She sat on the edge of the intake chair, hands folded tightly in her lap, waiting to see if anyone could help her navigate a world that had suddenly turned against her own skin.
